analysis.title: [GS] Midterms Playbook | 3x Webinars, 5x Ideas
key_insights: GS FICC & Equities baskets desk says the more actionable midterm question for investors is which policy areas become easier to negotiate, get more regulatory attention, or gain leverage in future spending debates, not which Democratic priorities become law.
The House passed a bipartisan continuing resolution funding the government through December 11, avoiding a shutdown in November.
Affordability is a common theme across Democratic and Republican agendas. The desk groups its five ideas around it.

ACA: the enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, which led to premium increases and lower marketplace participation. Providers face rising bad debt and uncompensated care as patients move to self-pay. The desk recommends a long ACA-exposed beneficiaries basket (GSHLCACA), recently rebalanced.

Drug pricing: both parties emphasize Medicare price negotiation expansion, Most-Favored-Nation benchmark pricing, a redefined exclusivity clock, and stricter Medicaid and PBM obligations. Democrats would likely raise the number of drugs selected for negotiation each year beyond the 20 scheduled for 2029. The desk recommends shorting a drug-makers basket (GSHLCBPH).

Power inflation: the Democratic AI and energy agenda calls for 'ratepayer protection', shifting AI power infrastructure costs from households to datacenters. The desk calls this one of the more underappreciated election-sensitive themes in US equities. The debate is moving from whether datacenters get built to who pays for the added generation and transmission.

Government spending: Congress has run on continuing resolutions rather than full appropriations since the end of the Biden administration. Republicans want more defense spending without matching increases elsewhere, while Democrats want parity between defense and domestic spending. The desk sees scope for non-defense spending debate to build into the December CR expiry.

Corporate tax: the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act made several TCJA business provisions permanent, including 100% bonus depreciation, and the 21% statutory rate was already permanent. Because President Trump can still veto legislation, the midterms are unlikely to change tax law. 2027-28 earnings are largely insulated, and the risk is to valuations beyond 2029.
Antitrust: Democratic leaders have criticized the administration's antitrust controls, and the desk sees potential for stricter Big Tech oversight. The desk suggests shorting Big Tech.

Financial regulation: Democrats have focused on rebuilding CFPB authority and Wall Street oversight, which could dampen bullish momentum in Financials. The desk suggests shorting investment banks and crypto-exposed equities.

Tariffs: Democrats would have limited ability to reverse tariffs while Trump is in office, and he continues to implement tariffs under alternative authorities after the Supreme Court invalidated the IEEPA tariffs. The desk sees more risk of tariffs rising than falling between now and early 2027, and suggests shorting tariff-sensitive equities.

Housing: Congress passed bipartisan housing-supply legislation in 2026. Democrats could differentiate through expanded housing tax credits and first-time homebuyer incentives, but large fiscal measures still need presidential approval. The desk suggests going long homebuilders.
GS is hosting three midterm webinars on November 4-5 (SGT): an election first take, a trading floor and D.C. view, and an election post-mortem.

sector_views.rationale: Restoring enhanced ACA subsidies would return patient volumes and reduce bad debt and uncompensated care.
Bipartisan drug-pricing pressure, with named drugs at MRK and AMGN identified for price setting starting in 2028, points to lower projected US sales.
Policy convergence on who bears datacenter power costs could give utilities and grid operators regulatory clarity.
Datacenter cost-bearing rules would make the economics of some projects less attractive. The desk suggests buying protection.
Democrats push for parity between defense and domestic spending, which would limit defense increases.

sector_views.sector: Non-defense government contractors and research institutions
sector_views.rationale: They are the primary beneficiaries of broader non-defense spending increases.
A less favorable regulatory backdrop could dampen capital market activity.
Tariff risk is skewed higher through early 2027.
Possible expanded housing tax credits and first-time buyer incentives.

earnings_insights: The desk says 2027-28 earnings are largely insulated from corporate tax changes under either election outcome.
MRK and AMGN have identified drugs that could undergo Medicare price setting starting in 2028, leading to a projected decline in US sales.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Moving to a higher rate would reduce after-tax income for full-rate payers. The desk sees the risk to valuations beyond 2029, not to 2027-28 earnings.
A November shutdown is avoided. The December expiry is the next spending catalyst.

crypto_views: Crypto-exposed equities are suggested as a short because Democratic financial regulation and CFPB oversight could bring a less favorable regulatory backdrop.

risk_factors: Policy outcomes are limited by the presidential veto, so a Democratic House or Senate gains agenda and oversight control, not new law.
A move from the 21% corporate rate to a higher one would reduce after-tax income for full-rate payers, with the valuation risk beyond 2029.
Tariffs may rise rather than fall between now and early 2027.
The December 11 continuing resolution expiry could revive spending and shutdown debate.
The legislation tying US drug prices to international benchmarks is described in ALGS filings as 'drastic and unprecedented'.
